accepted_examples.german: Wir müssen über dieses Produkt genauer Bescheid wissen.
accepted_examples.english: We need some more information about that product.
accepted_examples.note: Bescheid wissen is an idiomatic construction meaning to know or have information about something; the translation is idiomatic.

accepted_examples.german: Das war auch mein erster Gedanke.
accepted_examples.english: That was the first thing I thought about, too.
accepted_examples.note: The sentence uses the singular lemma Gedanke in a natural and direct sense.

accepted_examples.german: Kunihiko traf das Ziel mit seinem ersten Schuss.
accepted_examples.english: Kunihiko hit the target with his first shot.
accepted_examples.note: Ziel is the direct object meaning target, and the English sentence matches.

accepted_examples.german: Nicht aussteigen, solange das Fahrzeug noch in Bewegung ist!
accepted_examples.english: Don't get off while the vehicle is in motion.
accepted_examples.note: In Bewegung sein is a natural phrase meaning to be in motion.

accepted_examples.german: Ich mag es, wenn die Fenster offen sind.
accepted_examples.english: I like it when the windows are open.
accepted_examples.note: Offen is correctly used predicatively after sind.

accepted_examples.german: Ist das wirklich alkoholfreies Bier?
accepted_examples.english: Is this really a non-alcoholic beer?
accepted_examples.note: The sentence illustrates Bier and its compound alkoholfrei correctly.

accepted_examples.german: Alle außer dir kamen mit einem Partner.
accepted_examples.english: Everyone except you came with a partner.
accepted_examples.note: Partner is used with the target sense and the translation is direct.

accepted_examples.german: Er steckte Maria den Ring an den Finger.
accepted_examples.english: He put the ring on Mary's finger.
accepted_examples.note: The sentence uses Finger in the intended body-part sense.

accepted_examples.german: Lass Tom nicht weg, ehe ich da bin!
accepted_examples.english: Don't let Tom leave before I get there.
accepted_examples.note: Ehe correctly introduces a subordinate clause meaning before.

accepted_examples.german: Das war die letzte Rolle Klopapier.
accepted_examples.english: That was the last roll of toilet paper.
accepted_examples.note: Rolle means a roll in the paper-product context.

accepted_examples.german: Als ich dort ankam, war Tom schon wach.
accepted_examples.english: Tom was awake by the time I got there.
accepted_examples.note: Wach is correctly used as a predicative adjective.

accepted_examples.german: Mein Chef ist doppelt so alt wie ich.
accepted_examples.english: My boss is twice as old as I am.
accepted_examples.note: Chef is used in its common workplace sense.

accepted_examples.german: Die Arbeit war schon erledigt, bevor ich ankam.
accepted_examples.english: The work had been completed before I arrived.
accepted_examples.note: Erledigt describes the work as completed; the English translation preserves the result state.

accepted_examples.german: Hoffentlich komme ich nicht in den Stau.
accepted_examples.english: I hope I don't get stuck in traffic.
accepted_examples.note: Hoffentlich is correctly rendered with an English hope clause.

accepted_examples.german: Ich kann nicht so gut tanzen wie Tom.
accepted_examples.english: I can't dance as well as Tom does.
accepted_examples.note: The infinitive tanzen follows the modal verb kann and the translation matches.

accepted_examples.german: Wir wollen uns ein neues Zuhause kaufen.
accepted_examples.english: We want to buy a new home.
accepted_examples.note: The sentence and translation both use Zuhause as a place to live.

accepted_examples.german: Es ist wunderbar, wieder da zu sein.
accepted_examples.english: It's wonderful to be back.
accepted_examples.note: Wunderbar is correctly used predicatively with the infinitive clause.

accepted_examples.german: Man vergleicht das Leben oft mit einer Reise.
accepted_examples.english: Life is often compared to a journey.
accepted_examples.note: Reise is used as the object of mit and the translation matches the journey sense.

accepted_examples.german: Sie benimmt sich nicht wie eine Dame.
accepted_examples.english: Her manners are not those of a lady.
accepted_examples.note: Dame is used in its sense of a woman associated with refined manners.

accepted_examples.german: Hättest du Lust, irgendwann mal essen zu gehen?
accepted_examples.english: Would you like to go out to dinner sometime?
accepted_examples.note: Irgendwann mal naturally means sometime in this invitation.

held_examples.german: Geben Sie einen Schuß Rum dazu.
held_examples.reason: Uses obsolete spelling Schuß; replaced with a newly written example using current spelling.

held_examples.german: Darüber habe ich mir noch keine Gedanken gemacht.
held_examples.reason: Uses the plural Gedanken and does not directly show the singular headword; a more direct singular example was selected.

held_examples.german: Du zielst zu niedrig auf das Ziel.
held_examples.reason: The wording repeats the target-root and is awkward; a natural target example was selected.

held_examples.german: Ich bin froh, daß Sie mein Anwalt sind.
held_examples.reason: Uses obsolete spelling daß and is less suitable as a straightforward current example; replaced with a concise example.

held_examples.german: Halt die Klappe und hör mir zu!
held_examples.reason: This vulgar idiom means shut up and does not illustrate the entry's literal flap/lid sense.

held_examples.german: Tom und Maria haben ein schönes Zuhause.
held_examples.reason: The English translation incorrectly says their home is beautiful instead of saying they have a beautiful home.

held_examples.german: Ich habe nicht genügend Geld für eine Reise.
held_examples.reason: The translation uses travel as a verb and does not match the German noun phrase for a trip.

held_examples.german: Er ist stolz, den Preis gewonnen zu haben.
held_examples.reason: The example uses gewonnen as part of a perfect infinitive, while this entry is categorized as an adjectival participle.

editorial_examples.german: Der Kuchen enthält einen Schuss Rum.
editorial_examples.english: The cake contains a splash of rum.
editorial_examples.note: New current-spelling example written for the rum sense; replaces a candidate with obsolete ß spelling.
Original current-spelling example for the lawyer sense.

editorial_examples.english: The flap on the mailbox is stuck.
editorial_examples.note: Original neutral example for the literal flap sense; the entry gloss has been broadened to include the common literal and colloquial senses.

editorial_examples.german: Das gewonnene Geld ging an die Schule.
editorial_examples.english: The money won went to the school.
editorial_examples.note: Original example uses gewonnen as an attributive past participle, matching this entry's adjectival classification.

entry_updates.note: Replace an excessively narrow and obscure translated Wiktionary sub-sense with the common literal meanings and clearly label the idiomatic colloquial sense.

plural_reviews.value: Usually singular in this directional sense
plural_reviews.note: West in the sense of the cardinal direction or region is normally singular; Weste is a separate noun meaning vest.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Usually singular for the direction or region; Weste is an unrelated noun meaning vest.

plural_reviews.note: Mum forms the plural Mums.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Mums is the standard plural form.

plural_reviews.note: Realität forms the plural Realitäten.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Realitäten is used for multiple realities or distinct factual situations.

plural_reviews.note: Duden lists Öffentlichkeiten as the plural form.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Plural can refer to distinct publics or public spheres.

plural_reviews.note: Duden lists both Verdächte and Verdachte as nominative plural forms.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Both Verdächte and Verdachte are standard plural forms.

plural_reviews.note: For the material sense, Zucker is normally used without a plural; Duden lists Zucker for different kinds or varieties.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Usually a mass noun with no plural in everyday use; Zucker can refer to distinct varieties.

plural_reviews.note: Magen forms the plural Mägen.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Standard plural: Mägen.

plural_reviews.note: Duden lists Tunnel as the usual plural and Tunnels as a less frequent variant.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Tunnel is the usual plural; Tunnels is less frequent.

plural_reviews.note: Applause is a valid but rare plural form.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Plural is rare; Applause is the form listed by Duden.

plural_reviews.note: Markt forms the plural Märkte.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Standard plural: Märkte.

plural_reviews.note: For masculine der Pack meaning a small bundle, Duden lists Packe and the rare variant Packs.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Packe is the usual plural; Packs is rare. The neuter homograph has a separate sense.

plural_reviews.note: Bereich forms the plural Bereiche.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Standard plural: Bereiche.

plural_reviews.note: Viertel is unchanged in the nominative plural; Vierteln is a declined dative plural form, not a separate plural lemma.
plural_reviews.usage_note: The plural lemma is Viertel; Vierteln occurs in the dative plural.

plural_reviews.note: For the masculine sense meaning psychological or medical shock, Schocks is standard; Schocke is marked obsolete.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Use Schocks; Schocke is obsolete in this sense.

plural_reviews.note: Empfang forms Empfänge when referring to multiple receptions or receiving events.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Plural: Empfänge; use for distinct receptions or receiving events.

plural_reviews.note: Miete forms the plural Mieten.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Plural: Mieten.

plural_reviews.note: Duden gives Hauptleute as the main plural and Hauptmänner as a variant used outside the military.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Hauptleute is the main plural; outside the military, Hauptmänner is also used.

plural_reviews.note: Mäuse is a plural-only colloquial noun meaning money in this sense.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Plural-only colloquial slang for money; singular Maus normally means the animal.

plural_reviews.note: Duden lists both forms in technical usage; Stäube is also used for different kinds of dust.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Usually a mass noun; Staube and Stäube occur in technical usage, especially for distinct dust types.

plural_reviews.note: For the farmer sense, Bauer is a weak masculine noun and forms Bauern.
plural_reviews.usage_note: For a farmer, the plural is Bauern.

plural_reviews.note: Duden lists Geliebten and the shorter variant Geliebte in suitable plural contexts for the substantivized adjective.
plural_reviews.usage_note: The common plural with a determiner is Geliebten; Geliebte occurs without an article, for example zwei Geliebte.

plural_reviews.note: For das Steuer meaning steering control or rudder, the plural is unchanged Steuer.
plural_reviews.usage_note: The plural stays Steuer; do not confuse the neuter steering sense with feminine die Steuer meaning tax, plural Steuern.

plural_reviews.note: Duden lists Kilo and Kilos as plural variants.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Kilo and Kilos are both accepted plural forms.

plural_reviews.note: For the masculine shield or buckler sense, the plural is Schilde; the neuter sign sense has a different plural, Schilder.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Schilde is for der Schild (shield); das Schild (sign) forms Schilder.
